sets.name: Superpowers
sets.blurb: A working method for coding agents: ask what the person really wants, write a plan, test first, find the cause of a bug before fixing it, and prove it works before saying so. This is what makes small models far more dependable.
sets.author: Jesse Vincent (obra)
sets.note: Trimmed to six skills that need no extra tools. Subagent and git-worktree skills are left out.

skills.name: brainstorming
skills.description: You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, modifying behavior, or planning anything new, in software or out of it (a talk, a business, a renovation).

skills.name: systematic-debugging
skills.description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes

skills.name: test-driven-development
skills.description: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code

skills.name: using-superpowers
skills.description: Use when starting any conversation - establishes how to find and use skills, requiring skill invocation before ANY response including clarifying questions

skills.name: verification-before-completion
skills.description: Use when about to claim work is complete, fixed, or passing, before committing or creating PRs - requires running verification commands and confirming output before making any success claims; evidence before assertions always

skills.name: writing-plans
skills.description: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code

sets.name: Shoggoth basics
sets.blurb: Skills written for Shoggoth: diagrams that appear as pictures in the chat, and clear Markdown for documents.
sets.author: Shoggoth

skills.name: diagrams
skills.description: Draw diagrams as Mermaid code that Shoggoth shows as a picture in the chat. Use whenever the user asks for a diagram, flowchart, sequence diagram, architecture sketch, ER diagram, state machine, timeline, mind map or any picture of how things connect.

skills.name: markdown-writing
skills.description: Write clear Markdown for chat replies and for files such as README, notes, docs, changelogs, meeting notes and plans. Use when the user asks you to write, draft, rewrite, tidy or structure a document or text, or when you are about to save a .md file.

sets.name: My skills
sets.blurb: Skills you made or copied in yourself. Put a folder with a SKILL.md file in /home/user/zest/zd/skills/mine and it appears here.

recommended.label: Best small model
recommended.take: Very fast, runs on almost anything, and calls tools well. Its answers are short and to the point. Give it web search in a harness such as OpenChamber and it is the smartest small model I have used. Think of it as a stand-in for a cloud “flash” model.

recommended.label: Best all-rounder
recommended.take: Very fast and competent at everyday tasks. It sometimes mangles complex code, but you can run it again and again until it gets there. It does well at research, tweaking system settings and scripts, and at agent work (better than GLM). A good in-editor helper for small functions. Its writing style is not to everyone's taste.

recommended.label: Only if you can't run Qwen 3.6
recommended.take: Fast, but a confident bluffer: it makes things up often, so I would not trust it to write code. It improves a lot when you give it skills in a harness like OpenCode or Hermes, but pick it only if Qwen 3.6 is out of reach.

recommended.label: Clear and concise
recommended.take: I like the style: clear, concise and competent. It is simply slow next to the mixture-of-experts models.

recommended.label: A thinker
recommended.take: Competent, but it ruminates and refines its answers before it replies, and can think for ages unless you tell it to keep its thinking and answers short.

first_run.blurb: Answers fast and keeps it short. Runs on almost any computer.
My general pick: fast, and good at everyday tasks, research and simple code.
The most capable, for a big computer. It takes a couple of minutes to start.

library.title: Make any model better: a harness and skills
library.blurb: A model gets much more useful when it can search the web and follow skills.

tools.name: OpenChamber
tools.take: The app I recommend for working with your models. Connect it through the [Server](#server) page. I find Unsloth Desktop laggy at the moment, and Hermes more complex than most people need.

tools.name: obra/superpowers
tools.take: Give your models a few skills, especially this set, and most of them turn into a very good daily driver. A trimmed copy already comes with Shoggoth: switch it on under [Skills](#skills).

connect.help: Save this as `opencode.json` in your project, or add the `shoggoth` part to your existing config.
In Hermes, choose a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint and enter these three values.

tools.name: llama.cpp server
tools.take: The engine underneath most local AI. Shoggoth comes with a ready example: run `providers new llama-server --from llama-server` and follow [the ten-minute guide](https://github.com/yudhanjaya/Zest/blob/main/docs/ENGINES.md).

tools.name: Luke's Dev Lab
tools.take: Speed and agent tests of local models on real hardware: how fast they decode, how they handle long prompts, and whether they finish real tasks.

tools.name: Artificial Analysis
tools.take: Compares models on overall quality, speed and price side by side. Good for a quick overall ranking.

tools.name: LMArena
tools.take: People vote blind between two answers. It shows which models people actually prefer for everyday chat.

tools.name: Aider leaderboards
tools.take: How well models edit code in real projects. Look here if you want a coding helper.

tools.name: Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard
tools.take: How reliably models call tools and functions. This matters when you give a model web search or other tools.

tools.name: SWE-bench
tools.take: Whether a model can fix real bugs from GitHub projects. A tough test for coding agents.

tools.name: LiveBench
tools.take: Reasoning, maths, coding and language questions that are refreshed often, so models can't simply have memorised the answers.

tools.name: BenchLM
tools.take: Collects benchmark scores for many models in one place, so you can compare them side by side.

tools.name: LLM Stats
tools.take: Lists the benchmarks themselves and which models lead on each, with an explanation of what every test measures.

tools.name: r/LocalLLaMA
tools.take: People running models at home share what works on real computers. Good for first impressions of a new release.

tools.name: Level1Techs forum: Deep Machine Learning / AI
tools.take: Enthusiasts and engineers discussing hardware and local AI setups, with real-world speeds and troubleshooting.
